title: Signs that need emergency help
text: Some signs mean you should get emergency help straight away instead of waiting: struggling to breathe or being unable to speak, blue or very pale lips, tongue, face or skin, coughing up blood, collapsing or fainting, and sudden confusion or unusual sleepiness.

title: Struggling to breathe
text: Struggling to breathe, such as gasping, choking or being unable to speak a full sentence, is an emergency. Call your local emergency number or go to an emergency department straight away.

title: Blue, pale or blotchy skin
text: Blue, pale or blotchy skin, lips or tongue, or feeling cold and sweaty with pale blotchy skin, are warning signs that need emergency help straight away.

title: Sudden confusion or unusual sleepiness
text: Sudden confusion, such as not knowing where you are, or becoming very sleepy is a reason to get emergency help. Confusion can be an early sign of a chest infection, especially in older people.

title: Coughing up blood
text: Coughing up blood is listed by the NHS and by Asthma + Lung UK as a reason to get emergency help.

title: Collapse or fainting
text: Collapsing or fainting is a reason to get emergency help, according to Asthma + Lung UK.
source_name: Asthma + Lung UK: What is pneumonia?

title: How to get emergency help
text: In an emergency, do not drive yourself. Ask someone to drive you, or call your local emergency number and ask for an ambulance. Bring the medicines you take, or a list of them.

title: Higher-risk result without emergency signs
text: When a checklist or scan points to higher risk but there are no emergency signs, the sensible step is to be seen by a doctor promptly, in person, through an urgent appointment, an urgent-care service or a hospital, rather than waiting to see if it passes. If an emergency sign appears, treat it as an emergency.
source_name: Project wording based on the NHS urgent-versus-emergency advice

title: Signs that call for an urgent appointment
text: Coloured phlegm, chest pain that comes and goes or happens when breathing or coughing, or feeling short of breath are reasons to ask for an urgent appointment with a doctor or to call a health helpline.

title: What a Routine result means
text: A Routine result means nothing in the information provided raised concern for this tool. It does not mean nothing is wrong. If symptoms continue or get worse, speak to a doctor, and watch for emergency signs.

title: What Routine, Review soon and Urgent mean
text: Routine, Review soon and Urgent are priority labels for the order in which a clinician should look at a case. They are not diagnoses. Urgent means it should be looked at promptly, Review soon means a clinician should review it but it is less pressing, and Routine means nothing in the information raised concern.

title: Who is more likely to become seriously ill
text: Babies, older people and people with heart or lung conditions are more likely to become seriously ill with pneumonia and may need treatment in hospital. Being over 65, or being very unwell, are also reasons for a doctor to consider hospital care.

title: The CRB-65 checklist
text: CRB-65 is a four-item checklist doctors use to judge how serious a pneumonia may be: new confusion, fast breathing (30 or more breaths a minute), low blood pressure, and age 65 or over. Each item scores one point. A score of 0 suggests lower risk, 1 or 2 suggests hospital assessment should be considered, and 3 or 4 suggests urgent hospital admission.
source_name: GPnotebook summary of the British Thoracic Society CAP guideline (CRB65, pulse oximetry)

title: Low oxygen reading
text: British Thoracic Society guidance treats an oxygen saturation below 92 percent on a pulse oximeter as a sign that hospital assessment is needed.
source_name: GPnotebook summary of the British Thoracic Society CAP guideline (CRB65, pulse oximetry)

title: What pneumonia is
text: Pneumonia is inflammation of the lungs, usually caused by an infection.

title: Common symptoms
text: Common symptoms include a cough, shortness of breath, a high temperature, chest pain, an aching body, feeling very tired, loss of appetite and wheezing. They can start suddenly or build up over a few days.

title: What causes pneumonia
text: Pneumonia is usually caused by a bacterial or viral infection. It can sometimes follow another infection such as flu, RSV or COVID-19.

title: How pneumonia is treated
text: Treatment depends on what caused the pneumonia and how unwell someone is, and a clinician decides it. Some people recover at home, while others need hospital care, where extra oxygen can be given to help breathing. Most people get better within 2 to 4 weeks.

title: Recovery
text: Recovery is different for everyone. Many people feel better 2 to 4 weeks after starting treatment, but full recovery can take 6 months or more.

title: General self-care advice
text: General NHS advice is to rest until you feel better, drink plenty of fluids, cover your mouth and nose when you cough or sneeze, put used tissues in the bin quickly, wash your hands often, and avoid smoking. Ask a clinician before taking any medicines.

title: Vaccines
text: Vaccines are available against some infections that can lead to pneumonia, such as flu, pneumococcal infection, RSV and COVID-19. A clinician or pharmacist can say which are recommended for a particular person.

title: The role of a chest X-ray
text: A chest X-ray and blood tests may be used to check for pneumonia or other conditions. A clinician interprets the results together with the person's symptoms.

title: Babies and children
text: Babies and young children can become seriously ill with pneumonia, and a baby who is floppy or cannot be woken needs emergency help. This tool was built mostly on adult X-rays, so a child should always be seen by a clinician.

title: Why missing information matters
text: If breathing rate, blood pressure or confusion were not provided, the tool cannot rule out higher risk. It treats missing answers as unknown, never as normal, and will not confirm a Routine result. A clinician can measure these quickly.

title: What the imaging percentage means
text: The imaging percentage estimates how much the scan resembles pneumonia-like opacity in the research data the model learned from. It is not a diagnosis, and it can be wrong, especially for children, unusual images and very small findings.

title: What the heatmap shows
text: The coloured heatmap shows the area the model focused on. It is approximate and is not proof of where a problem is. In testing it matched the radiologists' marked areas no better than a typical-location guess, so it is shown only for scans flagged Urgent.

title: Small findings can be missed
text: The imaging model is more likely to miss small or faint findings: in testing, the cases it missed had smaller marked areas than the ones it caught. A normal-looking result does not rule out illness.

title: Lying-down versus standing X-rays
text: X-rays taken lying in bed (AP) and standing (PA) look different, and in testing the model was less reliable on standing (PA) films. If the view is unknown, the tool uses stricter settings, so more cases are flagged for review.

title: What this tool is and is not
text: This is a research prototype for decision support. It does not diagnose, prescribe or replace a clinician. Its guidance comes from UK sources, and local guidance may differ. If you are worried, speak to a clinician.

title: Questions worth asking a clinician
text: Useful questions for a clinician: What could explain this scan? Do I need other tests, such as blood tests or a repeat X-ray? Which symptoms should make me come back sooner? How long should recovery take? Does any health condition I have raise my risk?
